claim: Many tasks used to study decision-making encourage subjects to integrate evidence over time.
source: Many tasks used to study decision-making encourage subjects to integrate evidence over time.
evidence: This is a general statement about decision-making tasks in the field, drawing from established scientific knowledge.

claim: Several commonly accepted signs of integration were also predicted by non-integration strategies.
source: Several commonly accepted signs of integration were also predicted by non-integration strategies.
evidence: This claim is supported by the simulations and analyses presented in the manuscript showing that non-integration models can mimic integration.

claim: An integration model could fit data generated by non-integration models.
source: Furthermore, an integration model could fit data generated by non-integration models.
evidence: This is demonstrated through simulations in the manuscript where integration models are fit to data generated by extrema detection and snapshot models.

claim: A non-integration strategy was falsified in each human subject tested.
source: In human subjects performing the task, we falsified a non-integration strategy in each and confirmed prolonged integration in all but one subject.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data and model comparisons presented for the six human subjects.

claim: Prolonged integration was confirmed in all but one human subject.
source: In human subjects performing the task, we falsified a non-integration strategy in each and confirmed prolonged integration in all but one subject.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data and model fitting results showing integration time-constants for five of six subjects.

claim: The presence of noise in sensory stimuli encourages subjects to reduce it by integrating the sensory information over time.
source: The presence of this noise encourages subjects to reduce it by integrating the sensory information over time.
evidence: This is based on established principles of signal processing and decision theory.

claim: A subject may not integrate sensory evidence when making decisions, even though they are encouraged to do so.
source: One concern is that a subject may not integrate sensory evidence when making these decisions, even though they are encouraged to do so.
evidence: This is a theoretical concern that motivates the study.

claim: The concern about non-integration is exacerbated in animal subjects because they must learn the task without explicit instructions.
source: The concern is exacerbated in animal subjects because they must learn the task without explicit instructions.
evidence: This is based on logical inference about the differences between human and animal experimental paradigms.

claim: Integration models predict that subjects' decisions appear to incorporate evidence presented throughout the entire stimulus presentation epoch in fixed stimulus duration tasks.
source: Integration models predict several observations that are common in behavioral data: in fixed stimulus duration (FSD) tasks, subjects' decisions appear to incorporate evidence presented throughout the entire stimulus presentation epoch (e.g. Odoemene et al., 2018; Deverett et al., 2018; Morcos and Harvey, 2016; Katz et al., 2016; Yates et al., 2017; Wyart et al., 2012)
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies showing this pattern.

claim: In variable stimulus duration tasks, accuracy improves with increasing stimulus duration.
source: in variable stimulus duration (VSD) tasks, accuracy improves with increasing stimulus duration (e.g. Britten et al., 1992; Gold and Shadlen, 2000; Kiani et al., 2008; de Lafuente et al., 2015; Kiani and Shadlen, 2009; Bowman et al., 2012; Brunton et al., 2013; Robertson et al., 2012)
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple empirical studies.

claim: In free response tasks, RTs for the most difficult stimulus conditions are longer than those for easier stimulus conditions.
source: and, in free response (FR) tasks, RTs for the most difficult stimulus conditions are longer than those for easier stimulus conditions (e.g. Roitman and Shadlen, 2002; see Ratcliff and McKoon, 2008 for review)
evidence: This is supported by citations to empirical studies and a review.

claim: Models that posit little to no integration can fit data from FR tasks.
source: For example, previous work has shown that models that posit little to no integration can also fit data from FR tasks (Ditterich, 2006; Thura et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The integration model posits that noisy evidence is sequentially sampled from a stationary distribution and is perfectly integrated.
source: It posits that noisy evidence is sequentially sampled from a stationary distribution of random values representing the noisy momentary evidence from the stimulus and is perfectly integrated (i.e. with no leak).
evidence: This is a description of the model used in the study.

claim: In the integration model, the decision can be terminated either when the integrated evidence exceeds one of two decision-bounds or when the stimulus is extinguished.
source: The decision can be terminated in two ways: either the integrated evidence exceeds one of two decision-bounds (the timing of which determines the decision's duration) or the stimulus is extinguished.
evidence: This is a description of the model's decision termination rules.

claim: In the extrema detection model, evidence is sampled sequentially but not integrated.
source: In the extrema detection model, evidence is sampled sequentially from a stationary distribution until a sample exceeds one of two decision-bounds, which terminates the decision. Crucially, however, the sampled evidence is not integrated.
evidence: This is a description of the extrema detection model used in the study.

claim: In the extrema detection model, evidence that does not exceed a decision-bound is ignored and forgotten.
source: Evidence that does not exceed a decision-bound has no effect on the decision; it is ignored and forgotten.
evidence: This is a description of how the extrema detection model processes evidence.

claim: In the extrema detection model, if the evidence stream extinguishes before an extremum is detected, then the choice is made independent of the evidence.
source: If the evidence stream extinguishes before an extremum is detected, then the choice is made independent of the evidence (i.e. random guessing).
evidence: This is a description of the extrema detection model's guessing rule.

claim: In the snapshot model, the decision-maker acquires a single sample of evidence at a random time during the stimulus presentation.
source: The decision-maker acquires a single sample of evidence at a random time during the stimulus presentation.
evidence: This is a description of the snapshot model.

claim: The extrema detection and snapshot models can produce sigmoidal psychometric curves whose slope matched that of the integration model.
source: As shown in Figure 2A, the extrema detection and snapshot models can produce sigmoidal psychometric curves whose slope matched that of the integration model.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the simulation results shown in Figure 2A.

claim: All three models produced psychophysical kernels that are effectively indistinguishable in fixed stimulus duration tasks.
source: Given the simulated choice-data, all three models produced psychophysical kernels that are effectively indistinguishable (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the simulation results shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Non-integration models can match the choice-accuracy of the integration model because of the lack of constraints on how the sensory stimulus is transformed into a signal-to-noise ratio.
source: First, they can match the choice-accuracy of the integration model because of the lack of constraints on how the sensory stimulus is transformed into a signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) of the momentary evidence.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the modeling results about why non-integration models can mimic integration.

claim: Extrema detection and snapshot can compensate for being highly suboptimal by adopting higher SNR.
source: This bestows extrema detection and snapshot with the ability to produce choice-accuracy that matches that of integration; while these models are highly suboptimal compared to the integration model, they can compensate by adopting higher SNR (Figure 2A, inset).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the simulation results showing different κ parameters for the models.

claim: Snapshot can produce a flat psychophysical kernel because the data analyst is free to assert any distribution of sampling times.
source: Snapshot can produce a flat kernel—and theoretically any other kernel shape—because the data analyst is free to assert any distribution of sampling times.
evidence: This is an inference about the flexibility of the snapshot model.

claim: In extrema detection, the sample of evidence that determines the choice is exponentially distributed in time.
source: Indeed, in extrema detection, the sample of evidence that determines the choice is exponentially distributed in time (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a mathematical property of the extrema detection model.

claim: Extrema detection and snapshot predict that sensitivity should improve with increasing stimulus duration in VSD tasks.
source: We simulated VSD data with either an extrema detection model or a snapshot model (with an exponential sampling distribution). The figure shows that the sensitivity of both models improved with increasing stimulus duration, although sensitivity plateaued for the longer stimulus durations (data points in Figure 3A and B, respectively).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the simulation results shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: The improvement of sensitivity in extrema detection and snapshot models is attributed to the guessing mechanisms posited by the models.
source: Unlike integration, the extrema detection and snapshot models do not improve their sensitivity by averaging-out noise. Instead, the improvement of sensitivity is attributed to the guessing mechanisms posited by the models.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the modeling results about the mechanism underlying sensitivity improvement.

claim: The integration model provided an excellent account of the simulated extrema detection dataset in VSD tasks.
source: Qualitatively, integration provided an excellent account of the simulated extrema detection dataset.
evidence: This is based on the model fitting results shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The fit of the integration model to the simulated snapshot dataset was noticeably worse than to the extrema detection dataset.
source: The fit of the integration model to the simulated snapshot dataset was noticeably worse (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is based on the model fitting results shown in Figure 3B.

claim: For both extrema detection and snapshot generated datasets, a model comparison favored the data-generating model over the integration model.
source: For both datasets, a model comparison unsurprisingly favored the data-generating model over the integration model (ΔBIC=−70.34 when extrema detection generated the data; ΔBIC=−182.79 when snapshot generated the data).
evidence: This is based on the BIC model comparison statistics calculated from the fits.

claim: Extrema detection predicts that RT should depend on the stimulus strength in FR tasks.
source: First, extrema detection also predicts that RT should depend on the stimulus strength (Figure 4A, top; see also Ditterich, 2006): the weaker the stimulus strength, the more samples it takes for an extremum to be detected.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the simulation results and supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The snapshot model does not predict that RT depends on stimulus strength in FR tasks.
source: In contrast, the snapshot model does not predict this—and hence does not mimic integration—because the time at which a sample is acquired is independent of stimulus strength.
evidence: This is an inference based on the properties of the snapshot model.

claim: Integration can successfully predict choice-accuracy from mean RTs, even when data were generated by an extrema detection model.
source: Second, it is possible for integration to successfully predict choice-accuracy from mean RTs, even though the data were generated by an extrema detection model.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the simulation results shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Integration and extrema detection are not distinguishable on the basis of the shapes of the RT distributions.
source: Finally, integration and extrema detection are not distinguishable on the basis of the shapes of the RT distributions.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the simulation results shown in Figure 4B and C.

claim: The extrema detection model posits decision times that are exponentially distributed.
source: As described earlier, the extrema detection model posits decision times that are exponentially distributed.
evidence: This is a mathematical property of the extrema detection model.

claim: After convolving the exponential decision time distribution with the Gaussian non-decision time distribution, the resulting RT distribution is similar to that of the integration prediction.
source: However, after convolving the exponential decision time distribution with the Gaussian non-decision time distribution, the resulting RT distribution is similar to that of the integration prediction and to what is typically observed in data (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the simulation results shown in Figure 4B and C.

claim: All but one dataset with 1000 trials per stimulus strength yielded strong support for the data-generating model.
source: In contrast, all but one dataset with 1000 trials per stimulus strength (12,000 trials in total) yielded strong support for the data-generating model.
evidence: This is based on the model comparison results from the systematic simulation study.

claim: Extrema detection predicts shorter decision times and longer non-decision times compared to integration.
source: While extrema detection and integration predict similar RT distributions, extrema detection predicts shorter decision times and longer non-decision times.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the simulation results shown in Figure 4B and C.

claim: The difference in non-decision time between extrema detection and integration is robust and typically ranges from 50 to 150 ms.
source: Importantly, the difference in non-decision time is robust and typically ranges from 50 to 150 ms.
evidence: This is based on the simulation results comparing the two models.

claim: SNR in a FR task ought to be closely matched to that in a VSD task, so long as properties of the sensory stimulus are unchanged.
source: Instead, we reasoned that SNR in a FR task ought to be closely matched to that in a VSD task, so long as properties of the sensory stimulus are unchanged.
evidence: This is a logical inference about how SNR should behave across task designs.

claim: If a subject makes decisions that are so automatic that the decision times are negligible, then the resulting RTs would reflect only the non-decision time.
source: If a subject makes decisions that are so automatic that the decision times are negligible, then the resulting RTs would reflect only the non-decision time and hence confer an empirical estimate of the non-decision time distribution.
evidence: This is a logical inference about how to estimate non-decision time.

claim: With the non-decision time constrained, only the data-generating model succeeds in fitting and predicting the data in simulations.
source: With the non-decision time constrained, only the data-generating model succeeds in fitting and predicting the data.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the simulation results shown in Figure 5B-E.

claim: Six human subjects performed the motion discrimination task.
source: Six human subjects performed the motion discrimination task.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental procedure.

claim: Stronger motion led to more accurate and faster choices in FR trials.
source: As expected, stronger motion led to more accurate and faster choices in FR trials (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is based on the experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: In VSD trials, longer stimulus durations were associated with greater sensitivity.
source: In VSD trials, longer stimulus durations were associated with greater sensitivity (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is based on the experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The speeded decision trials gave rise to similar non-decision time estimates across the six subjects.
source: The speeded decision trials gave rise to similar non-decision time estimates across the six subjects (black arrows, top row of Figure 6A; Table 1)
evidence: This is based on the experimental data shown in Figure 6A and Table 1.

claim: With constraints on the non-decision time and κ parameter, extrema detection was incompatible with each subject's dataset.
source: With constraints on the non-decision time and κ parameter, extrema detection was incompatible with each subject's dataset.
evidence: This is based on the model fitting results shown in Figure 6 and Tables 1 and 2.

claim: Extrema detection produced visibly poor fits to the mean RTs in many cases.
source: Extrema detection produced visibly poor fits to the mean RTs in many cases, and in all cases fit the mean RTs worse than integration (Table 1).
evidence: This is based on the model fitting results shown in Figure 6A and Table 1.

claim: The extrema detection model systematically underestimated the slope of the choice function when predicting choice-data.
source: Additionally, the model systematically underestimated the slope of the choice function when predicting choice-data.
evidence: This is based on the model prediction results shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The extrema detection model's fits to the VSD trials were visibly poor for four of the six subjects.
source: With κ constrained, the extrema detection model's fits to the VSD trials were visibly poor for four of the six subjects (dashed cyan curves in Figure 6B).
evidence: This is based on the model fitting results shown in Figure 6B.

claim: For every subject, extrema detection failed at least one of the benchmarks.
source: Nevertheless, for every subject, extrema detection failed at least one of the benchmarks described above.
evidence: This is a summary of the model fitting results across all subjects.

claim: For subjects 1-3, the integration model's ability to fit and predict data despite rigid constraints was remarkable.
source: In contrast, we found strong evidence in favor of the integration model for some of the subjects. For subjects 1-3, the model's ability to fit and predict data despite rigid constraints was remarkable.
evidence: This is based on the model fitting results shown in Figure 6.

claim: Integration was heavily favored over extrema detection when fitting the full RT distributions for all subjects.
source: Finally, integration was heavily favored over extrema detection when fitting the full RT distributions (Table 2).
evidence: This is based on the BIC model comparison statistics shown in Table 2.

claim: For subjects 2 and 3, the time-constants estimated by the leaky integration model were effectively infinite.
source: For subjects 2 and 3, the time-constants were effectively infinite.
evidence: This is based on the leaky integration model fitting results shown in Figure 7A.

claim: For subjects 2 and 3, the leaky integration model was functionally equivalent to the perfect integration model.
source: As such, the leaky integration model was functionally equivalent to the perfect integration model.
evidence: This is an inference based on the estimated time-constants being effectively infinite.

claim: For subjects 4 and 5, the leaky integration model produced time-constants that were just below 1 s.
source: In subjects 4 and 5, the model produced time-constants that were just below 1 s (0.80 s for subject 4, 0.84 s for subject 5; Figure 7A)
evidence: This is based on the leaky integration model fitting results shown in Figure 7A.

claim: For subjects 4 and 5, the addition of the leak parameter substantially improved the quality of the model fit.
source: and the addition of the leak parameter substantially improved the quality of the model fit (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is based on the BIC model comparison results shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The leaky integration model failed to account for data from subject 6.
source: Finally, the leaky integration model failed to account for data from subject 6.
evidence: This is based on the model fitting results shown in Figure 7.

claim: Several observations interpreted as conclusive evidence for integration were also predicted by non-integration strategies.
source: Simulations of these models in different task-designs showed that several observations interpreted as conclusive evidence for integration were also predicted by non-integration strategies.
evidence: This is a summary of the simulation results presented in the manuscript.

claim: The integration model consistently fit simulated data well, even when these data were generated by non-integration models.
source: Additionally, the integration model consistently fit simulated data well, even when these data were generated by non-integration models.
evidence: This is based on the model fitting results from the simulations.

claim: The first model that attempted to reconcile accuracy with reaction time resembles the extrema detection model.
source: In fact, the first model that attempted to reconcile accuracy with reaction time resembles our extrema detection model (Cartwright and Festinger, 1943).
evidence: This is supported by citation to historical work.

claim: Similar non-integration mechanisms, known as probability summation, have long been used to explain the detection of static stimuli.
source: Similar non-integration mechanisms, known as probability summation, have long been used to explain the detection of static stimuli as a function of their intensity, duration, and spatial properties (e.g. Sachs et al., 1971; Watson, 1979; Robson and Graham, 1981).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work on probability summation.

claim: Bounded evidence integration is optimal for decisions based on sequences of independent samples.
source: A parallel line of research showed that bounded evidence integration is optimal for decisions based on sequences of independent samples (Barnard, 1946; Wald, 1947; Good, 1979).
evidence: This is supported by citations to theoretical work on optimal decision-making.

claim: A crucial factor that allowed non-integration models to mimic integration was the freedom of the models to fit the SNR of the momentary evidence to the data.
source: A crucial factor was the freedom of the models to fit the SNR of the momentary evidence to the data.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the modeling results about why non-integration models can mimic integration.

claim: Non-integration models are highly suboptimal compared to integration and therefore require higher SNR to produce the same level of performance.
source: Non-integration models are highly suboptimal compared to integration and therefore require higher SNR to produce the same level of performance.
evidence: This is an inference based on the properties of the models.

claim: There is a trade-off between the SNR of the momentary evidence and the efficiency with which evidence samples are combined.
source: In other words, there is a trade-off between the SNR of the momentary evidence and the efficiency with which evidence samples are combined.
evidence: This is an inference about the relationship between SNR and integration efficiency.

claim: The SNR can be adequately constrained if its estimate is derived from a separate task-design.
source: We demonstrate that the SNR can be adequately constrained if its estimate is derived from a separate task-design (see also Drugowitsch et al., 2016).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the experimental results and supported by citation to previous work.

claim: In FSD and VSD task-designs, non-integration models mimicked integration in part because of a guessing mechanism.
source: In FSD and VSD task-designs, we found that non-integration models mimicked integration in part because of a guessing mechanism.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the modeling results.

claim: Extrema detection mimics integration in a FR task in part because the non-decision time is unconstrained.
source: In agreement with Ditterich, 2006, we found that extrema detection mimics integration in a FR task in part because the non-decision time is unconstrained.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the modeling results and supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Given fits to the same dataset, extrema detection predicts longer non-decision time than integration.
source: Given fits to the same dataset, extrema detection predicts longer non-decision time than integration.
evidence: This is based on the modeling results comparing the two models.

claim: Experimenters should not assume subjects integrate evidence just because integration is the optimal strategy.
source: At the very least, experimenters should not assume subjects integrate evidence just because integration is the optimal strategy.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the findings of the study.

claim: A given behavioral observation should be adduced as conclusive evidence for an integration strategy only if it is not reproduced by alternative strategies.
source: The results also imply that a given behavioral observation should be adduced as conclusive evidence for an integration strategy only if it is not reproduced by alternative strategies.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the findings of the study.

claim: If data generated by a non-integration strategy were misattributed to an integration strategy, an experimenter might mistake short bursts of neural activity for a mechanism of integration.
source: For example, if data generated by a non-integration strategy were misattributed to an integration strategy, an experimenter might mistake short bursts of neural activity for a mechanism of integration
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential consequences of misattribution.

claim: If neural responses clearly reflect integrated evidence, then it would be reasonable to presume that the subjects' decisions were based on integrated evidence.
source: More broadly, if neural responses clearly reflect integrated evidence (e.g. Huk and Shadlen, 2005), then it would be reasonable to presume that the subjects' decisions were based on integrated evidence.
evidence: This is a logical inference supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The misidentification of decision strategy leads to parameter fits that are systematically misleading.
source: We showed that the misidentification of a subject's decision strategy leads to parameter fits that are systematically misleading.
evidence: This is based on the modeling results showing different parameter estimates for different models.

claim: Fits of the integration model to simulated data generated by extrema detection led to an underestimate of both SNR and non-decision time.
source: For example, fits of the integration model to simulated data generated by extrema detection led to an underestimate of both SNR and non-decision time.
evidence: This is based on the modeling results comparing parameter estimates.

claim: Integration models are often useful even in the absence of evidence for an integration strategy.
source: We wish to emphasize that integration models are often useful even in the absence of evidence for an integration strategy.
evidence: This is a statement about the utility of integration models as descriptive tools.

claim: Integration models can be used as descriptive models of behavioral data.
source: They can be used as descriptive models of behavioral data.
evidence: This is a statement about the utility of integration models.

claim: The constraints on SNR and non-decision time allowed the authors to rule-out a non-integration strategy for each subject tested.
source: The constraints allowed us to rule-out a non-integration strategy for each subject we tested
evidence: This is based on the experimental results and model comparisons.

claim: SNR in visual cortex would have to be implausibly high in order for a non-integration strategy to be viable in a RDM task.
source: which is consistent with the idea that SNR in visual cortex would have to be implausibly high in order for a non-integration strategy to be viable in a RDM task (Ditterich, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Strong evidence for effectively perfect integration was found in half of the subjects.
source: We found strong evidence for effectively perfect integration in half of our subjects.
evidence: This is based on the experimental results showing infinite time-constants for three subjects.

claim: In three subjects, the predictions of the perfect integration model were remarkably accurate, even with strong parameter constraints.
source: In these subjects, the predictions of the perfect integration model were remarkably accurate, even with strong parameter constraints.
evidence: This is based on the model fitting results for subjects 1-3.

claim: Data from two of the remaining three subjects appeared to lie somewhere between the predictions of perfect integration and no integration.
source: Data from two of the remaining three subjects appeared to lie somewhere between the predictions of perfect integration and no integration
evidence: This is based on the model fitting results for subjects 4 and 5.

claim: Fits of a leaky integration model were consistent with the observation that subjects 4 and 5 integrated with only minimal information loss.
source: and fits of a leaky integration model were consistent with this observation. The time-constants estimated by the leaky integration model suggested that these subjects integrated with only minimal information loss.
evidence: This is based on the leaky integration model fitting results showing time-constants just below 1 s.

claim: No model tested offered a satisfactory explanation of the data from subject 6.
source: Surprisingly, no model we tested offered a satisfactory explanation of the data from subject 6.
evidence: This is based on the model fitting results for subject 6.

claim: The time-constants estimated for the 'leaky' subjects are likely underestimated.
source: Furthermore, the time-constants are likely underestimated.
evidence: This is an inference based on the potential bias in non-decision time estimates.

claim: The estimates of the non-decision time are biased toward longer times because the authors assume decision time is negligible in the speeded decision experiment.
source: Our estimates of the non-decision time are biased toward longer times because we assume decision time is negligible in the speeded decision experiment
evidence: This is an inference about the potential bias in the non-decision time estimates.

claim: An overestimate of the non-decision time would lead to an underestimate of the time-constant.
source: and an overestimate of the non-decision time would lead to an underestimate of the time-constant.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the relationship between non-decision time and time-constant estimates.

claim: The apparent variability in decision strategy across subjects underscores the importance of analyzing data at the level of individuals.
source: While the small number of subjects we used prevents us from making sweeping claims, the apparent variability in decision strategy across our subjects underscores the importance of analyzing data at the level of individuals.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the variability observed across subjects.

claim: A subject's strategy could lie somewhere between no integration and perfect integration or in a completely different space of models.
source: A subject's strategy could lie somewhere between no integration and perfect integration or in a completely different space of models.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the range of possible decision strategies.

claim: A subject may change their strategy depending on several factors, including the task structure, the nature of the stimulus, and the subject's training history.
source: A subject may also change their strategy depending on several factors, including the task structure, the nature of the stimulus, and the subject's training history (Brown and Heathcote, 2005 ; Evans and Hawkins, 2019; Tsetsos et al., 2012; Glaze et al., 2015; Ossmy et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work showing strategy variability.

claim: Pinto et al. (2018) showed that a snapshot strategy predicted a linear psychometric function under certain conditions in their task, which did not match the mice's behavioral data.
source: For example, Pinto et al. (2018) tasked mice with counting the number of visual 'pulses' that appeared as the mice ran through a virtual corridor. The authors showed that a snapshot strategy predicted a linear psychometric function under certain conditions in their task, which did not match the mice's behavioral data.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Waskom and Kiani (2018) were able to rule-out a non-integration strategy for humans performing a contrast discrimination task.
source: Additionally, Waskom and Kiani (2018) were able to rule-out a non-integration strategy for humans performing a contrast discrimination task.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Ditterich (2006) showed that the SNR in visual cortex would have to be implausibly high in order for a non-integration strategy to explain data from a RDM discrimination task.
source: Finally, as mentioned above, Ditterich (2006) showed that the SNR in visual cortex would have to be implausibly high in order for a non-integration strategy to explain data from a RDM discrimination task.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Any attempt to differentiate integration from non-integration strategies requires that the latter be considered in the first place.
source: Nevertheless, any attempt to differentiate integration from non-integration strategies requires that the latter be considered in the first place.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the necessity of considering alternative models.

claim: The general approach developed in this study should be widely applicable to many evidence integration tasks.
source: The general approach should be widely applicable to many evidence integration tasks, although it will likely require modifications.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the generalizability of the approach.

claim: The approach explicitly mitigates the factors that allow non-integration strategies to mimic integration.
source: It explicitly mitigates the factors that allow non-integration strategies to mimic integration and allow integration models to fit data generated by alternative mechanisms.
evidence: This is a description of how the approach works based on the findings.
